meta.title: Who really said "He’s a Writer for the Ages—For the Ages of Four to Eight"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Probably not Dorothy Parker. The earliest version, from 1938, credits the critic George Jean Nathan — and Quote Investigator credits him only provisionally.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He's a Writer for the Ages—For the Ages of Four to Eight'?
meta.ogDescription: The 1938 original is George Jean Nathan’s, about plays and the ages five to twelve. Parker’s name arrives ten years later, in Bennett Cerf’s 1948 anecdote book.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — provisionally George Jean Nathan
answer.authorDates: 1882–1958 · American drama critic and magazine editor
answer.sourceLine: The earliest version of this joke that anyone has found runs in the “Patter” column of the Reader’s Digest in January 1938, and it is credited to the drama critic George Jean Nathan: “Mr. ———— writes his plays for the ages — the ages between five and twelve.” The wording on this page — a writer, and the ages four to eight — first appears ten years later, in Bennett Cerf’s 1948 anecdote collection, where it is already attached to Parker. Quote Investigator ↗ says it “would provisionally credit Nathan,” and we do not go further than that.
answer.confidenceText: Provisionally credited — the earliest evidence points to Nathan, but no source shows him using this exact wording.

source.excerpt: Mr. ———— writes his plays for the ages — the ages between five and twelve
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ is the anchor. It locates the earliest instance in the January 1938 Reader’s Digest, credited to Nathan, and concludes: “currently the earliest evidence in 1938 suggests that the quip was crafted by George Jean Nathan. The first linkage to Dorothy Parker was printed ten years later by Bennett Cerf in 1948.”

The credit then splits, and stays split for decades. Nathan is named again by Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949), by a Saturday Review literary quiz in 1951, and by a Seattle newspaper as late as 1983. Parker is named by Bennett Cerf ↗ in 1948 and again in his 1957 column, by The Algonquin Wits in 1968, and by Time in 1987.

Cerf is the weak link in the Parker chain, and QI flags it: having published the “four to eight” version in 1948, he printed a different upper limit — “the ages of four to six” — in his 1957 newspaper column, still crediting Parker. A source that cannot keep its own quotation stable is thin ground for an attribution.

We looked for independent support on Parker’s side and found none: Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page ↗ does not carry the line in any section. Wikiquote’s George Jean Nathan page ↗ does not carry it either — so Nathan’s claim rests on QI’s 1938 citation and the later compilers, not on a sourced quotation page.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1938 wording, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the Reader’s Digest’s “Patter” column. Note what it is not: it is about a playwright rather than a novelist, and the ages are five to twelve. The familiar “four to eight” form is a later reshaping, and no source we or QI can point to shows Nathan using it.

author.name: George Jean Nathan
author.heading: About George Jean Nathan
author.metaLine: 1882–1958 · American drama critic and magazine editor
author.bio: George Jean Nathan (14 February 1882 – 8 April 1958) was the most feared American drama critic of his generation and, with H. L. Mencken, co-founder and co-editor of The Smart Set and The American Mercury. His reviewing style was exactly the register this joke lives in: compressed, contemptuous and built for reprinting. That is also why the joke could migrate — a Nathan-shaped insult is a Parker-shaped insult, and only one of those names is still a household word.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely contested rather than simply wrong, and the honest answer has two halves: the joke is probably Nathan’s, and the sentence you have read is probably Cerf’s reshaping of it.

items.why: Parker’s name first appears on the joke in Bennett Cerf ↗’s Shake Well Before Using (1948), a decade after the earliest printing. Wikiquote’s Parker page ↗ does not carry the line at all.
Quote Investigator ↗ finds the joke in the January 1938 Reader’s Digest credited to Nathan, and names him again in 1949, 1951 and 1983 citations. It credits him “provisionally” — and so do we.
Cerf printed “the ages of four to eight” in 1948 and “the ages of four to six” in his 1957 column, crediting Parker both times. The exact sentence on this page has no source older than him.

misattribution.truthLine: The safest true statement is the narrow one: the joke is documented from 1938 as George Jean Nathan’s, and nobody has produced a Parker source older than a 1948 anecdote book — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a pun on a critic’s highest compliment. To call someone “a writer for the ages” is to say the work will outlast its moment; the second half yanks the word “ages” from eternity down to a reading level. It is a complete review in eleven words, which is why it has been recycled for nearly ninety years.

It is also why the attribution slid. A line this portable gets retold before it gets sourced, and each retelling is free to change the target from a playwright to a novelist, the ages from five-to-twelve to four-to-eight, and the author from a critic nobody under sixty has heard of to the most quotable woman in American letters.
detailsBody: We are deliberately not resolving this one. Quote Investigator says it “would provisionally credit Nathan,” and the evidence really is provisional: the 1938 citation is a different sentence about a different kind of writer, and the sentence people actually quote has no attestation earlier than Bennett Cerf’s, which changed shape between his own two printings.

So the page credits Nathan and says why the credit is soft, rather than manufacturing a clean answer. If a pre-1938 printing ever turns up — or a Nathan text using the “four to eight” form — the picture changes, and we would rather be corrected than confident.
context.pull: A complete review in eleven words — which is why it has been recycled for ninety years.
